inverted_duplication.name: inverted_duplication
inverted_duplication.note: updated review request: is there any other sample that has the structural variant and does have orthogonal sequencing? if there is any orthogonal sequencing e.g. nanopore or pacbio it might make powerful completementary viz. previous agent notes NOT POSSIBLE FOR THIS EVENT, and that is checkable rather than a judgement. HGSV_2721 is a singleton in the ensemble callset (AC=1, N_HET=1 of 3202 genomes), so HG02768 is the only sample that carries it; and HG02768 is not in the 1000 Genomes ONT consortium release -- listing s3://1000g-ont PROCESSED_DATA/ALIGNED_TO_HG38/MINIMAP2_ALIGNED_BAMS/ gives 500 samples and HG02768 is not among them (HG02763 and HG02772 are the nearest ids). So there is no orthogonal long-read data of this locus in this individual to put beside the short reads. The site already carries the figure this idea describes, one event over: inversion_long_read is HG00151 chr1:197,787,660-197,788,855, the same 1KGP ensemble call with that sample's 1000G ONT minimap2 reads, where single reads span the inversion and split at both breakpoints instead of triangulating it from pair orientation. If the pairing is wanted at THIS locus it needs a different variant -- a non-singleton inversion or INVdup whose carriers intersect the 500 ONT samples -- which is a data-selection change, not a spec edit. STILL NOT POSSIBLE, and the answer is now checked against long-read cohorts rather than only against this sample's absence. Two sources exist and both say no. (1) 1KGP PacBio WGS (s3://1000g-ont/1KGP_PacBio_WGS) is 140 genomes, all GM/NA ids -- HG02768 is not among them -- and its integrated callset (disco_truvari_collapsed.deduped.vcf.gz) is assembly-based INS/DEL only: it contains no INV records anywhere on chr1, so it cannot even be asked who carries this one. (2) The 500 1000G-ONT samples DO have per-sample Sniffles v2.6.2 calls, which do emit INV and DUP. Queried all 500 at chr1:39,655,000-39,665,000 (hg38, the figure's window): zero INV or DUP calls in any of them. So there is no long-read genome, in either cohort, that carries this event and could be put beside the short reads. The site already carries the figure this idea describes one event over -- inversion_long_read, HG00151 chr1:197,787,660-197,788,855, the same 1KGP ensemble call with that sample's ONT reads spanning the inversion. Pairing THIS locus still needs a different variant, i.e. a data-selection change.

cookbook_multiwig.name: cookbook_multiwig
cookbook_multiwig.note: REBUILT rather than defended this time. Root cause of dull was measurable: scanning all 104 PUR bigWigs over the AMY1A window gives one flat integer copy number per sample, 1 to 4, and the three samples in the figure happened to sit on adjacent levels -- so the picture was three colored plateaus with nothing to compare. Two changes. Eight individuals instead of three, picked to cover every level and every step pattern the population has here (4 across the whole cluster, 4 over one block and 3 over the other, the reference-flat 2, and a lost copy at 1), on the Okabe-Ito palette the other multi-sample figures use. And the scale is pinned 0-5 on the display: autoscale is per row, so a sample that never leaves the baseline drew the same full-height plot as one with a real gain, which is what actually destroyed the comparison. Rendering moved multirowxy -> multirowline for the same reason: filled areas over flat integer plateaus paint each row as a solid bar whose only readable feature is its top edge. As step traces you read the level and where it steps. On the zarr suggestion: NOT used for this figure, deliberately. The section it illustrates is the subadapters-with-a-color-each recipe, and a MultiWiggleZarrAdapter track has no per-signal colors, so a zarr capture here would picture a different recipe than the one printed above it -- and the 2504-sample zarr cohort figure already exists as cnv1000g/zarr_cohort. pangenome/hprc_chm13_allele.note: BOTH DONE. NAMING THE PANES: done in the app rather than over it — each view carries a displayName now, so the headers read 'hg38 (GRCh38) - no coordinates for this sequence', 'HPRC release 2 graph, cut to that window' and 'T2T-CHM13v2.0 (hs1) - an ordinary interval'. The headers already fell back to assembly names ('hg38', 'Human (T2T-CHM13v2.0/hs1)'), which is presumably what was easy to miss between three panes; naming all three also removes the 'Untitled view' the graph sat under. REPEATS: added, on BOTH panes, and they are the same UCSC RepeatMasker annotation so the two are comparable — hg38's from jbrowse.org's tabix'd copy, hs1's from hgdownload's bigBed. (The spec's warning about hgdownload is about a whole-file GET of hs1.2bit; ranged bigBed reads over a 180 kb window answer with CORS in well under a second, measured.) The picture: the CHM13-only interval is a near-continuous run of repeat, almost all LINE/L1, where the GRCh38 window it attaches to is broken up. WHAT IT IS NOT is a gap GRCh38 never closed, which was worth ruling out before claiming a mechanism: UCSC's hg38 'gap' track has exactly one record past chr17:82.5 Mb and it is the terminal 10 kb telomere at 83,247,441. So this is a real insertion allele in a LINE-dense subtelomere, not an assembly hole. The hs1 gene lane is gone with the change — jbrowse.org/ucsc/hs1/hs1.gff.gz has nothing in this window, so it was 70 px of empty lane, which is the 'no gene in this region' half of the note.

orthofinder_synteny/vertebrates.note: this is unfortunately a fairly chaotic screenshot.  the alpha probably should be increased.  the last compaison with zebrafish is particularly scrambled, unclear if autodiagonalization is working there IMPROVED, and the zebrafish question is answered by measurement rather than opinion. The three OrthoFinder figures were the only multi-row synteny specs that never got the levers the others use, and all three now carry them: collapseEmptyRows (every row was spending ~90px on a 'No tracks active / Open track selector' block, five or six of them down the middle of the frame, more height than the ribbons had), the reclaimed space spent on 170-180px bands, and alpha 0.06 against the 0.2 default, since an orthogroup link is a hairline and tens of thousands of them at 0.2 saturate into one wash where a dense bundle and a lone scattered ortholog paint the same. drawCurves was rendered too and rejected: the bezier version is the prettier picture and the worse figure, because a curve leaves its chromosome vertically and only bends toward its partner mid-band, so the bundles braid where they cross and stop pointing at anything. AUTODIAGONALIZE IS RUNNING ON THAT LEVEL, checked against a rendered autoDiagonalize:false control: without it the rows sit in natural order (chicken 1..Z, zebrafish 1..25) and the upper bands lose their vertical bundling. What it cannot do is make that band diagonal, because the map is not one-to-one. Weighting each chromosome by its link count, a chromosome's single best partner holds 79% of its links chicken to frog, 50% human to chicken, 34% frog to gar and 33% gar to zebrafish: past the teleost genome duplication two thirds of every gar linkage group's orthologs land somewhere other than its best zebrafish partner, and no left-to-right ordering of either row can fix that. No filter rescues it either, dropping every multi-copy expansion would still leave ~13k of the band's ~17.8k links. build_orthofinder_synteny.sh now PRINTS this table per adjacent pair, so it is reproducible rather than my arithmetic, and the tutorial reads the bottom band as the measurement it is.

SEARCHED, and the convention it lands on is what the figure already does: GENESPACE riparian plots, the reference for this kind of picture, order chromosomes to maximise synteny with a reference, colour ribbons by that reference's chromosomes, and stack genomes in phylogenetic order, which is autoDiagonalize + colorBy reference + the spec's evolutionary row order. The wheat-specific convention is homoeologous-group ordering, and diagonalizing produces it unprompted (2A 2D 2B, 7D 7A 7B, 3A 3B 3D, ...). The one real difference is that a riparian plot draws SYNTENIC BLOCKS while this draws one line per ortholog, and that is the tutorial's premise (orthogroups carry no position), so it is the MCScan tutorial that has blocks to draw.
